rv.q: The play, directed with more emotional naturalism than stylized virtuosic flash by Daniel Sullivan, remains joyously mean-spirited.

In short, I’m not sure I believe these men really work together.
Cannavale is so good that, like his character, he can make us buy whatever he’s selling.
That said, the drama often seems to be happening elsewhere, just beyond the proscenium, and not among the actors on stage, however individually adept.
As the result, the play simmers when it wants to boil.
This performance places Shelly firmly and dominatingly at the center of “Glengarry,” which needs to be a tight ensemble piece.

But once Mamet's salesmen lose both their motivation and their bitter camaraderie, the play itself begins to fall apart. Instead of being a savage evocation of the limitations of the American dream it becomes a melancholy description of inadequacy. Deeply disappointing
This Glengarry Glen Ross is a reminder that when everything clicks in the theater—writing, acting, directing, design—the result can be transcendent.
It's not every day that you get to see such top-notch performers play hardball onstage, and their flashes of electricity sustain this imperfect Glengarry.
In Daniel Sullivan’s unevenly directed production, Pacino entertainingly holds the stage, winning laugh after laugh, but he makes a miscalculation fatal to the play’s core.
The wait was long, the expectation high — and the result, as a whole, deflating.
Worse still is that four weeks later, the heat seems to have almost entirely escaped from this balloon of a play, and it’s barely aloft.
Now in it’s second Broadway revival, "Glengarry" doesn’t quite hold up to the romance and ingenuity it once demonstrated.
